glossary.definition: The property that makes matter exert electric forces; it comes in positive and negative kinds, is quantized in units of $e$, and is conserved.
$e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, the magnitude of the charge on a proton or electron.
SI unit of charge; one coulomb is about $6.24\times10^{18}$ elementary charges.
A material in which some charges (usually electrons) move freely.
A material in which charges cannot move freely.
Separation of charge within a neutral object due to a nearby charge, which lets charged objects attract neutral ones.
Connecting a conductor to Earth, which can supply or absorb any amount of charge.
Charging a conductor without contact by polarizing it near a charged object and grounding it.
$F = k|q_1q_2|/r^2$ with $k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C², along the line joining two point charges.
$\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²), with $k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$.
The net force or field from several charges is the vector sum of the individual contributions.
A small positive charge used to probe an electric field without disturbing it.
Force per unit charge, $\vec E = \vec F/q_0$ (N/C = V/m); a point charge makes $E = k|q|/r^2$.
Two equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance; characterized by its dipole moment $p = qd$.
Curves tangent to $\vec E$, starting on positive and ending on negative charges, denser where the field is stronger; they never cross.
A field with the same magnitude and direction everywhere, as between large parallel plates.
The state of a conductor with no moving charges: $E = 0$ inside, excess charge on the surface, field perpendicular to the surface.
A conducting enclosure that shields its interior from external electric fields.
The amount of field passing through a surface, $\Phi_E = \int\vec E\cdot d\vec A$; $EA\cos\theta$ for a flat area in a uniform field.
A vector perpendicular to a surface with magnitude equal to its area; outward for closed surfaces.
$\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$: total flux out of a closed surface is proportional to the charge inside.
An imaginary closed surface chosen to apply Gauss's law, ideally matching the symmetry of the charge.
Energy of a configuration of charges; for two point charges $U = kq_1q_2/r$ (zero at infinity).
Potential energy per unit charge, $V = U/q$, in volts; a point charge gives $V = kq/r$.
SI unit of potential: $1\text{ V} = 1\text{ J/C}$.
The change in potential between two points, $\Delta V$; a charge crossing it gains or loses energy $q\Delta V$.
Energy gained by charge $e$ through 1 V: $1\text{ eV} = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ J.
A surface of constant potential; perpendicular to field lines, and no work is done moving along it.
Two conductors separated by an insulator, storing equal and opposite charges and electric energy.
$C = Q/V$, the charge stored per volt; set by geometry and dielectric.
SI unit of capacitance, $1\text{ F} = 1\text{ C/V}$.
An insulating material placed between capacitor plates; it polarizes, reducing the field and raising the capacitance.
The factor $\kappa$ by which a dielectric multiplies capacitance.
Energy per unit volume stored in a field: $u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$ for an electric field and $u_B = B^2/(2\mu_0)$ for a magnetic field.
Rate of charge flow, $I = dQ/dt$, in amperes; conventional current is the direction positive charge would move.
SI unit of current: $1\text{ A} = 1\text{ C/s}$.
The work per unit charge a source (battery, generator) does moving charge through it, $\mathcal{E}$, in volts.
The slow average velocity of charge carriers along a conductor, $v_d = I/(nqA)$.
$R = V/I$, in ohms: how strongly a component opposes current.
SI unit of resistance: $1\ \Omega = 1$ V/A.
$V = IR$ with constant $R$; obeyed by ohmic materials such as metals at fixed temperature.
Material property $\rho$ (Ω·m) with $R = \rho L/A$.
A material whose resistance drops to exactly zero below a critical temperature.
Conversion of electrical energy to heat in a resistance, at rate $I^2R$.
Current per unit cross-sectional area, $\vec J = nq\vec v_d = \vec E/\rho$.
Resistance $r$ inside a real source, which lowers its terminal voltage when current flows.
Voltage across a source's terminals, $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$.
Junction rule (currents in = currents out) and loop rule (sum of potential changes around a loop = 0).
The total current into a junction equals the total current out (charge conservation).
The sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation).
A low-resistance meter connected in series to measure current.
A high-resistance meter connected in parallel to measure potential difference.
Choosing a load resistance equal to the source's internal resistance to transfer maximum power.
The characteristic time of exponential change; $\tau = RC$ for an RC circuit, $L/R$ for an RL circuit.
A circuit that passes slow signal changes and blocks rapid ones; an RC filter has crossover near $1/(2\pi RC)$.
The field $\vec B$ that exerts forces on moving charges and currents; its field lines form closed loops from north to south poles.
SI unit of magnetic field: $1\text{ T} = 1$ N/(A·m). Earth's field is about $5\times10^{-5}$ T.
$\vec F = q\vec v\times\vec B$ on a moving charge (magnitude $|q|vB\sin\theta$); $\vec F = I\vec L\times\vec B$ on a wire.
The frequency $f = |q|B/(2\pi m)$ of a charge circling in a uniform magnetic field, independent of its speed.
A device that separates ions by mass using the radius $r = mv/(qB)$ of their paths in a magnetic field.
$\mu = NIA$ for a current loop; the torque in a field is $\tau = \mu B\sin\phi$.
A device in which magnetic torque on current loops produces rotation; a commutator keeps the torque in one direction.
$\mu_0 \approx 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A, the constant in magnetic field formulas (exact before the 2019 SI redefinition; now measured, but equal to $4\pi\times10^{-7}$ to about 10 digits).
A long coil of wire; inside, $B = \mu_0nI$, nearly uniform and along the axis.
A solenoid with an iron core, giving a strong magnetic field that can be switched on and off.
Describes materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) whose atomic magnetic moments align in domains, producing strong magnetization.
$d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec\ell\times\hat r}{r^2}$: the field contribution of a current element.
$\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec\ell = \mu_0I_{\text{enc}}$ for steady currents; used with symmetry to find magnetic fields. Maxwell added a displacement-current term for changing electric fields.
$\Phi_B = \int\vec B\cdot d\vec A$; $BA\cos\theta$ for a flat loop in a uniform field, in webers.
SI unit of magnetic flux, $1\text{ Wb} = 1\text{ T·m}^2$.
A changing magnetic flux induces an emf: $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$.
An induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change in flux that produced it.
The emf $BLv$ across a conductor of length $L$ moving at speed $v$ perpendicular to a field $B$.
A device that rotates coils in a magnetic field to produce an emf $NBA\omega\sin\omega t$.
Swirling induced currents in bulk metal exposed to changing flux; they heat the metal and oppose motion.
Two coils on a common core that change AC voltage in the ratio of turns: $V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p$.
$L$ in $\mathcal{E} = -L\,dI/dt$, in henries; for a solenoid $L = \mu_0N^2A/\ell$.
SI unit of inductance: $1\text{ H} = 1$ V·s/A.
A coil used for its inductance; it opposes changes in current and stores energy $\tfrac12LI^2$.
Current (and voltage) that varies sinusoidally, $V = V_0\sin\omega t$; 60 Hz in North America.
Root-mean-square value; for a sinusoid $V_{\text{rms}} = V_0/\sqrt2$, the steady value with the same average power.
Opposition of a capacitor ($X_C = 1/\omega C$) or inductor ($X_L = \omega L$) to AC, in ohms.
Total opposition to AC in a circuit; series RLC: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.
$I_d = \varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt$, the term Maxwell added to Ampère's law so that a changing electric field produces a magnetic field just as a current does.
The four laws of electromagnetism: Gauss's law, Gauss's law for magnetism ($\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec A = 0$), Faraday's law, and the Ampère–Maxwell law.
A self-sustaining wave of perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields, traveling at $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$ in vacuum.
The range of EM waves by wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible (400–700 nm), ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
$c = 3.00\times10^8$ m/s in vacuum, the same for all EM waves and all inertial observers.
A filter that transmits only the component of the electric field along its axis.
Describes light whose electric field oscillates in a single direction.
Polarized light through a polarizer at angle $\theta$ has $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$.
A line showing the direction light energy travels; the basis of geometric optics.
The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal.
$n = c/v$, the factor by which light slows in a material.
The bending of light as it crosses a boundary between materials with different speeds of light.
$n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$, with angles from the normal.
Dependence of the index of refraction on wavelength, which spreads white light into colors.
Complete reflection of light trying to pass into a lower-index medium at more than the critical angle.
The incidence angle with $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$ ($n_1 > n_2$) above which total internal reflection occurs.
Light travels between two points along the path of least time; it implies the laws of reflection and refraction.
An image from which light only appears to come; it cannot be projected on a screen ($d_i < 0$).
An image where light rays actually converge, which can be projected on a screen ($d_i > 0$).
A mirror curved inward that converges parallel rays to a focal point; $f = R/2 > 0$.
The point where rays parallel to the axis converge (or appear to diverge from) after a lens or mirror.
Distance from a lens or mirror to its focal point; positive for converging, negative for diverging optics.
A mirror curved outward; it diverges light, has $f < 0$, and forms virtual, upright, reduced images.
A lens thicker in the middle that brings parallel rays to a focus; $f > 0$.
A lens thinner in the middle that spreads parallel rays; $f < 0$.
$\dfrac1{d_o} + \dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f$, for thin lenses and spherical mirrors.
$m = h_i/h_o = -d_i/d_o$; negative means inverted.
$P = 1/f$ in diopters (m⁻¹).
$\dfrac1f = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac1{R_1} - \dfrac1{R_2}\right)$ for a thin lens in air (in a medium of index $n_m$, use $n/n_m - 1$).
Describes sources with a constant phase relationship, needed for a stable interference pattern.
The spreading of waves through openings or around obstacles comparable in size to the wavelength.
Many equally spaced slits producing sharp maxima at $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$.
Two point sources are just resolved at angular separation $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D$.
The laws of physics are the same in every inertial reference frame.
$\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} \ge 1$.
Time between two events measured by a clock present at both (at rest relative to them); the shortest measured interval.
Moving clocks run slow: $\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0$.
The length of an object measured in its own rest frame; the longest measured length.
Objects are shorter along their direction of motion: $L = L_0/\gamma$.
The energy $E_0 = mc^2$ a particle has by virtue of its mass.
Mass is a form of energy, $E_0 = mc^2$; nuclear reactions convert small mass changes into large energies.
$x' = \gamma(x - vt)$, $t' = \gamma(t - vx/c^2)$: how coordinates change between inertial frames.
A quantum of electromagnetic energy, $E = hf = hc/\lambda$, with momentum $h/\lambda$.
Emission of electrons from a metal by light; explained by photons, with $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$.
The minimum energy $\phi$ needed to free an electron from a metal's surface.
The lowest light frequency, $f_0 = \phi/h$, that can eject photoelectrons.
The set of discrete wavelengths emitted by an element's atoms, unique to that element.
The allowed energies of a bound system; for hydrogen $E_n = -13.6\text{ eV}/n^2$.
The lowest energy level of an atom or system ($n = 1$ in hydrogen).
The wavelength of a particle, $\lambda = h/p$.
Light and matter both show wave behavior (interference) and particle behavior (discrete quanta), depending on the experiment.
Position and momentum cannot both be sharply defined: $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge h/(4\pi)$.
A proton or neutron.
The number of protons $Z$ in a nucleus, which identifies the element.
The total number of nucleons $A = Z + N$.
Nuclei with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The very strong, short-range (~$10^{-15}$ m) attraction between nucleons that holds nuclei together.
$1\text{ u} = 1.6605\times10^{-27}$ kg, equivalent to 931.5 MeV.
The amount by which a nucleus's mass is less than the total mass of its separate nucleons.
Energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons, $E_B = \Delta m\,c^2$.
Splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter ones, releasing energy (about 200 MeV for uranium-235).
Joining of light nuclei into a heavier one, releasing energy; powers the Sun.
Emission of a helium-4 nucleus; $Z$ drops by 2 and $A$ by 4.
Emission of an electron (β⁻, $Z + 1$) or positron (β⁺, $Z - 1$) as a neutron and proton interconvert.
Emission of a high-energy photon as a nucleus drops to a lower energy state; $Z$ and $A$ unchanged.
Decays per second, $R = \lambda N$, in becquerels.
Time for half of a radioactive sample to decay, $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda$.
The average lifetime of an unstable nucleus, $\tau = 1/\lambda = T_{1/2}/\ln 2$.
The vector $\vec p = q\vec d$ of a dipole, pointing from $-q$ to $+q$; unit C·m.
A molecule with a permanent electric dipole moment, such as water.
A dipole created when an external field pulls an atom's or molecule's positive and negative charges apart; its moment is proportional to the field.
The transverse voltage that appears across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, as the magnetic force pushes carriers to one edge.
The voltage across a strip in the Hall effect, $V_H = v_dBw = IB/(nqt)$; its sign gives the sign of the carriers.
A small semiconductor chip that measures magnetic field through its Hall voltage, which is proportional to $B$.
The natural unit of atomic magnetic moment, $\mu_B = e\hbar/(2m_e) = 9.27\times10^{-24}$ J/T, about the spin moment of an electron.
Net magnetic dipole moment per unit volume of a material, $M$, in A/m; it adds $\mu_0M$ to the field.
The dimensionless $\chi_m$ in $\mu_0M = \chi_mB_0$: negative for diamagnets, small and positive for paramagnets, large for ferromagnets.
$K_m = \mu/\mu_0 = 1 + \chi_m$, the factor by which a material filling a solenoid multiplies its field.
A material's $\mu = K_m\mu_0$; inside a filled solenoid $B = \mu nI$.
The weak response of all materials in which induced atomic moments oppose an applied field; $\chi_m \approx -10^{-5}$, weakly repelled from strong fields.
Weak alignment of permanent atomic moments with an applied field against thermal agitation; small positive $\chi_m$ that falls with temperature.
For a paramagnet, the susceptibility is inversely proportional to absolute temperature, $\chi_m \propto 1/T$.
A region of a ferromagnet in which the atomic moments are all aligned.
The state of a ferromagnet whose domains are all aligned, so that further increases in the applied field add little magnetization (around 2 T for iron).
The lag of a ferromagnet's magnetization behind the applied field, so that the B-versus-applied-field curve forms a loop; the loop area is energy lost per cycle.
The magnetization a ferromagnet keeps after the applied field returns to zero; it is what makes a permanent magnet.
The temperature above which a ferromagnet loses its domains and becomes paramagnetic (770°C for iron).
$\vec S = \vec E\times\vec B/\mu_0$, the rate of electromagnetic energy flow per unit area (W/m²), pointing along the direction of energy flow.
Average power per unit area carried by a wave; for an EM wave $I = \tfrac12c\varepsilon_0E_0^2 = E_0B_0/(2\mu_0)$.
Pressure exerted by electromagnetic waves because they carry momentum: $I/c$ when absorbed, $2I/c$ when reflected straight back.
The depth at which an object under a flat surface appears, $(n_2/n_1)$ times its true depth; about 0.75 of the true depth seen from air into water.
The eye's change of lens shape to focus on objects at different distances.
The closest distance at which an eye can focus, about 25 cm for a young adult.
The farthest distance at which an eye can focus; infinity for a normal eye.
Having a far point closer than infinity; corrected with a diverging lens of focal length minus the far-point distance.
Having a near point farther than about 25 cm; corrected with a converging lens.
The ratio of the angle an image covers at the eye to the angle the object covers without the instrument; $M = 25\text{ cm}/f$ for a magnifier.
Two converging lenses: an objective that forms an enlarged real image and an eyepiece that magnifies it; $M = m_oM_e$.
The lens (or mirror) of a microscope or telescope nearest the object, which forms the first image.
The lens of a microscope or telescope nearest the eye, used as a magnifier to view the image formed by the objective.
An ideal object that absorbs all radiation falling on it; its thermal emission spectrum depends only on its temperature.
The peak wavelength of blackbody emission satisfies $\lambda_{\max}T = 2.898\times10^{-3}$ m·K.
The power radiated by a surface is $P = e\sigma AT^4$ with $\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/(m²·K⁴).
The fraction $e$ (0 to 1) of blackbody radiation that a surface emits at a given temperature; 1 for a blackbody.
The failure of classical physics, which predicted that blackbody intensity grows without limit at short wavelengths.
The blackbody spectrum $I(\lambda, T) = 2\pi hc^2/[\lambda^5(e^{hc/\lambda k_BT} - 1)]$, derived by quantizing oscillator energies in steps of $hf$.
The increase in wavelength of X-rays scattered by electrons, $\lambda' - \lambda = (h/m_ec)(1 - \cos\theta)$, explained by photon–electron collisions.
$h/(m_ec) = 2.43$ pm for the electron; the Compton shift at $90^\circ$.
The angle of incidence $\tan\theta_B = n_2/n_1$ at which reflected light is completely polarized parallel to the surface; reflected and refracted rays are then perpendicular.
The constant $M$ (in henries) linking two coils: a changing current in one induces $\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\,dI_1/dt$ in the other; the same in both directions.
In an AC circuit, the angle $\phi$ by which the current lags the source voltage; series RLC $\tan\phi = (X_L - X_C)/R$.
$\cos\phi = R/Z$ in an AC circuit; the average power is $P = I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi$.

references.title: Physical constants and data
references.body:
## Fundamental constants

| Quantity | Symbol | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Speed of light in vacuum | $c$ | $3.00\times10^8$ m/s |
| Gravitational constant | $G$ | $6.67\times10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg² |
| Elementary charge | $e$ | $1.602\times10^{-19}$ C |
| Coulomb constant | $k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$ | $8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C² |
| Permittivity of free space | $\varepsilon_0$ | $8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²) |
| Permeability of free space | $\mu_0$ | $4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A ($1.257\times10^{-6}$; measured since 2019, equal to $4\pi\times10^{-7}$ to 10 digits) |
| Planck's constant | $h$ | $6.63\times10^{-34}$ J·s $= 4.14\times10^{-15}$ eV·s |
| | $hc$ | $1240$ eV·nm |
| Boltzmann's constant | $k_B$ | $1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K |
| Gas constant | $R$ | $8.314$ J/(mol·K) |
| Avogadro's number | $N_A$ | $6.022\times10^{23}$ mol⁻¹ |
| Stefan–Boltzmann constant | $\sigma$ | $5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/(m²·K⁴) |
| Wien's displacement constant | $b$ | $2.898\times10^{-3}$ m·K |
| Compton wavelength of the electron | $h/(m_ec)$ | $2.43\times10^{-12}$ m |
| Bohr magneton | $\mu_B$ | $9.27\times10^{-24}$ J/T |

## Particle masses

| Particle | Mass (kg) | Mass (u) | Rest energy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electron | $9.11\times10^{-31}$ | 0.000549 | 0.511 MeV |
| Proton | $1.673\times10^{-27}$ | 1.007276 | 938.3 MeV |
| Neutron | $1.675\times10^{-27}$ | 1.008665 | 939.6 MeV |
| Hydrogen atom | | 1.007825 | |
| Atomic mass unit | $1.6605\times10^{-27}$ | 1 | 931.5 MeV |

## Earth, Moon, Sun

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Free-fall acceleration at Earth's surface | $g = 9.8$ m/s² (9.81 at sea level) |
| Mass of Earth | $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg |
| Radius of Earth | $6.37\times10^6$ m |
| Mass of Moon | $7.35\times10^{22}$ kg |
| Radius of Moon | $1.74\times10^6$ m |
| $g$ on the Moon | 1.62 m/s² |
| Mass of Sun | $1.99\times10^{30}$ kg |
| Earth–Sun distance | $1.50\times10^{11}$ m |
| Atmospheric pressure (sea level) | $1.013\times10^5$ Pa |

## Material data

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Density of water | 1000 kg/m³ |
| Density of air (sea level, 20°C) | 1.20 kg/m³ |
| Speed of sound in air (20°C) | 343 m/s |
| Specific heat of water | 4186 J/(kg·K) |
| Specific heat of ice | 2100 J/(kg·K) |
| Latent heat of fusion of water | $3.34\times10^5$ J/kg |
| Latent heat of vaporization of water | $2.26\times10^6$ J/kg |
| Resistivity of copper | $1.7\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m |
| Free-electron density of copper | $8.5\times10^{28}$ m⁻³ |
| Near point of a normal eye | 25 cm |
| Index of refraction: water, glass, diamond | 1.33, about 1.5, 2.42 |

references.title: Electricity, magnetism, optics, and modern physics
references.body:
## Electrostatics

| | |
|---|---|
| Coulomb's law | $F = k\dfrac{\lvert q_1q_2\rvert}{r^2}$ |
| Field | $\vec E = \vec F/q$; point charge $E = kq/r^2$ |
| Gauss's law | $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$ |
| Line, sheet | $E = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}$; $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ |
| Potential | $V = kq/r$; $U = kq_1q_2/r$; $\Delta U = q\Delta V$ |
| Dipole | $p = qd$; axis $E \approx 2kp/x^3$; $\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E$; $U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E$ |
| Field from potential | $\Delta V = -\int\vec E\cdot d\vec\ell$; $\vec E = -\nabla V$; uniform: $E = \Delta V/d$ |
| Capacitance | $C = Q/V$; parallel plates $C = \kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$ |
| Capacitor energy | $U = \tfrac12CV^2$; $u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$ |
| Combinations | parallel $C = \sum C_i$; series $1/C = \sum 1/C_i$ |

## Circuits

| | |
|---|---|
| Current, Ohm's law | $I = dQ/dt$; $V = IR$; $R = \rho L/A$ |
| Power | $P = IV = I^2R = V^2/R$ |
| Resistors | series $R = \sum R_i$; parallel $1/R = \sum 1/R_i$ |
| Real battery | $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ |
| Kirchhoff | $\sum I_{\text{in}} = \sum I_{\text{out}}$; $\sum\Delta V = 0$ around a loop |
| RC | $\tau = RC$; charging $q = C\mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$; discharging $q = Q_0e^{-t/\tau}$ |

## Magnetism and induction

| | |
|---|---|
| Force on charge | $F = \lvert q\rvert vB\sin\theta$; $\vec F = q\vec v\times\vec B$; $r = \dfrac{mv}{\lvert q\rvert B}$ |
| Force on wire | $F = ILB\sin\theta$; loop torque $\tau = NIAB\sin\phi$ |
| Straight wire | $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}$ |
| Loop center, solenoid | $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}$; $B = \mu_0nI$ |
| Hall effect | $V_H = v_dBw = \dfrac{IB}{nqt}$ |
| Magnetic materials | $B = K_mB_0$, $K_m = 1 + \chi_m$, $\mu = K_m\mu_0$; $B = B_0 + \mu_0M$ |
| Parallel wires | $F/L = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$ |
| Biot–Savart, Ampère | $d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec\ell\times\hat r}{r^2}$; $\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec\ell = \mu_0I_{\text{enc}}$ |
| Faraday | $\mathcal{E} = -N\dfrac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$, $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$; motional $\mathcal{E} = BLv$ |
| Transformer | $V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p$ |
| Inductance | $\mathcal{E} = -L\,dI/dt$; $U = \tfrac12LI^2$; RL $\tau = L/R$; mutual $\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\,dI_1/dt$ |
| LC, AC | $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$; $V_{\text{rms}} = V_0/\sqrt2$; $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$, $X_L = \omega L$; $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$ |
| Phase, power | $\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$; $P = I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi$, $\cos\phi = R/Z$ |

## Light and optics

| | |
|---|---|
| EM waves | $c = f\lambda = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$; $E = cB$; displacement current $I_d = \varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt$ |
| Wave energy | $u = \varepsilon_0E^2$; $\vec S = \vec E\times\vec B/\mu_0$; $I = \tfrac12c\varepsilon_0E_0^2 = \dfrac{E_0B_0}{2\mu_0}$; point source $I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}$ |
| Radiation pressure | $I/c$ absorbed; $2I/c$ reflected |
| Polarization | $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$; Brewster $\tan\theta_B = n_2/n_1$ |
| Refraction | $n = c/v$; $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$; $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$ |
| Mirrors and lenses | $\dfrac1{d_o} + \dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f$; $m = -\dfrac{d_i}{d_o}$; mirror $f = R/2$; $P = 1/f$ |
| Single surface | $\dfrac{n_1}{d_o} + \dfrac{n_2}{d_i} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$; $m = -\dfrac{n_1d_i}{n_2d_o}$ |
| Instruments | magnifier $M = \dfrac{25\text{ cm}}{f}$; microscope $M = m_o\dfrac{25\text{ cm}}{f_e}$; telescope $M = -\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}$ |
| Double slit, grating | $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (bright); $\Delta y = \lambda L/d$ |
| Single slit | $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (dark) |
| Resolution | $\theta_{\min} = 1.22\lambda/D$ |
| Thin film (one flip) | bright: $2nt = (m + \tfrac12)\lambda$ |

## Modern physics

| | |
|---|---|
| Relativity | $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}$; $\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0$; $L = L_0/\gamma$ |
| Velocity addition | $u = \dfrac{u' + v}{1 + u'v/c^2}$ |
| Energy, momentum | $E = \gamma mc^2$, $K = (\gamma - 1)mc^2$, $p = \gamma mv$, $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$ |
| Blackbody | $\lambda_{\max}T = 2.898\times10^{-3}$ m·K; $P = e\sigma AT^4$ |
| Photons | $E = hf = hc/\lambda$; $p = h/\lambda$ |
| Compton | $\lambda' - \lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$ |
| Photoelectric effect | $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$ |
| Hydrogen | $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6\text{ eV}}{n^2}$ |
| Matter waves | $\lambda = h/p$; $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge h/(4\pi)$ |
| Binding energy | $E_B = \Delta m\,c^2$ (1 u ↔ 931.5 MeV) |
| Decay | $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t} = N_0(\tfrac12)^{t/T_{1/2}}$; $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda$; $R = \lambda N$ |

drills.title: Charged particle circling in a magnetic field
drills.prompt: Consider {part} moving at ${vm}\times10^{{ve}}$ m/s perpendicular to a {B} T magnetic field. Find the magnetic force on it and the radius of its circular path, each to 3 significant figures. ($e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, $m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $m_p = 1.673\times10^{-27}$ kg)
drills.solution:
$F = |q|vB = (1.602\times10^{-19})({vm}\times10^{{ve}})({B}) = \mathbf{{F:texsci}}$ N.

$r = \dfrac{mv}{|q|B} = \dfrac{({mcoef:sig4}\times10^{{mexp}})({vm}\times10^{{ve}})}{(1.602\times10^{-19})({B})} = \mathbf{{r:texsci}}$ m.

drills.title: Force on a current-carrying wire
drills.prompt: A straight wire {L} m long carries {I} A in a uniform {B} T magnetic field. The wire makes an angle of {th}° with the field. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it, in newtons to 3 significant figures?
drills.solution: $F = ILB\sin\theta = ({I})({L})({B})\sin {th}^\circ =$ **{F:sig3} N**, perpendicular to both the wire and the field.

drills.title: Mass spectrometer radius
drills.prompt: A singly charged ion of mass {A} u ($1\text{ u} = 1.661\times10^{-27}$ kg) is accelerated from rest through {V:dp0} V and enters a {B} T magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity. Find its speed (m/s) and the radius of its path (cm), each to 3 significant figures. ($e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C)
drills.solution:
$m = {A}(1.661\times10^{-27}) = {m:texsci}$ kg. From $\tfrac12mv^2 = eV$: $v = \sqrt{2eV/m} = \mathbf{{v:texsci}}$ m/s.

$r = \dfrac{mv}{eB} = {r:texsci}$ m $=$ **{rcm:sig3} cm**.

drills.title: Magnetic field of a long straight wire
drills.prompt: A long straight wire carries {I:dp0} A. Find the magnetic field {rcm} cm from it, in microtesla to 3 significant figures. ($\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
drills.solution: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})({I:dp0})}{2\pi({rcm}/100)} = {B:texsci}$ T $=$ **{BuT:sig3} μT**.

drills.title: Field inside a solenoid
drills.prompt: A long solenoid {lcm} cm long has {N:dp0} turns and carries {I} A. Find the number of turns per meter and the magnetic field inside (in mT), each to 3 significant figures. ($\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
drills.solution:
Turns per meter: $n = \dfrac{\,N}{\ell} = \dfrac{{N:dp0}}{{lcm}/100\text{ m}} =$ **{n:sig3} turns/m**.

$B = \mu_0nI = (4\pi\times10^{-7})({n:sig4})({I}) =$ **{BmT:sig3} mT**. Use turns per meter, not the total number of turns.

drills.title: Force between parallel wires
drills.prompt: Two long parallel wires {dcm} cm apart carry {I1} A and {I2} A in the same direction. Find the force per meter between them in mN/m, to 3 significant figures. (Then decide: is it attractive or repulsive?)
drills.solution: $\dfrac FL = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{(2\times10^{-7})({I1})({I2})}{{dcm}/100} =$ **{FmN:sig3} mN/m**, attractive (currents in the same direction attract).

drills.title: Hall voltage and drift speed
drills.prompt: A strip of {mat} is {wcm} cm wide and {tmm} mm thick. It carries {I} A along its length, in a {B} T field perpendicular to its face. Find the Hall voltage (V) and the electrons' drift speed (m/s), each to 3 significant figures. ($e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C)
drills.solution:
The thickness along $\vec B$ is what matters: $V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt} = \dfrac{({I})({B})}{({nn:texsci})(1.602\times10^{-19})({tmm}\times10^{-3})} = \mathbf{{VH:texsci}}$ V.

$v_d = \dfrac{\,I}{nqA} = \dfrac{{I}}{({nn:texsci})(1.602\times10^{-19})({wcm}\times10^{-2})({tmm}\times10^{-3})} = \mathbf{{vd:texsci}}$ m/s. Check: $v_dBw$ gives the same Hall voltage.

drills.title: Solenoid with a ferromagnetic core
drills.prompt: A solenoid {lcm} cm long has {N:dp0} turns and carries {I} A. Find the field inside (a) when it is empty, in mT, and (b) when it is filled with iron of relative permeability {Km:dp0}, in T. (c) Find the iron's magnetization in A/m. Give each to 3 significant figures. ($\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
drills.solution:
$n = \dfrac{{N:dp0}}{{lcm}/100\text{ m}} = {n:sig4}$ turns/m.

(a) $B_0 = \mu_0nI = (4\pi\times10^{-7})({n:sig4})({I}) =$ **{B0mT:sig3} mT**.

(b) $B = K_mB_0 = {Km:dp0}({B0mT:sig4}\text{ mT}) =$ **{B:sig3} T**.

(c) $M = \dfrac{B - B_0}{\mu_0} = (K_m - 1)nI = ({Km:dp0} - 1)({n:sig4})({I}) = \mathbf{{M:texsci}}$ A/m.

drills.title: Induced emf in a coil
drills.prompt: A {N:dp0}-turn coil of area {A:dp3} m² lies perpendicular to a magnetic field that changes steadily from {B1} T to {B2} T in {t} s. Find the magnitude of the induced emf (V) and, if the coil's resistance is {R} Ω, the induced current (A), each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$|\Delta\Phi_B| = |{B2} - {B1}|({A:dp3})$ Wb per turn.

$|\mathcal{E}| = N\dfrac{|\Delta\Phi_B|}{\Delta t} =$ **{emf:sig3} V**; $I = \mathcal{E}/R =$ **{I:sig3} A**, directed to oppose the change in flux.

drills.title: Sliding rod on rails
drills.prompt: A rod {L} m long slides at {v} m/s along conducting rails in a {B} T field perpendicular to the rails. The rails are joined by a {R} Ω resistor. Find the emf (V), the current (A), and the force (N) needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed, each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\mathcal{E} = BLv = ({B})({L})({v}) =$ **{emf:sig3} V**; $I = \mathcal{E}/R =$ **{I:sig3} A**.

The field pushes back on the current with $F = ILB$, so you must push with **{F:sig3} N** (power $Fv = I^2R$).

drills.title: Ideal transformer
drills.prompt: An ideal transformer has {Np:dp0} primary turns and {Ns:dp0} secondary turns, with {Vp:dp0} V (rms) on the primary. Find the secondary voltage (V) and, if the secondary delivers {Is} A, the primary current (A), each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$V_s = V_p\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = {Vp:dp0}\cdot\dfrac{{Ns:dp0}}{{Np:dp0}} =$ **{Vs:sig3} V**.

Power is conserved: $I_p = \dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_p} =$ **{Ip:sig3} A**.

drills.title: RL circuit current growth
drills.prompt: A {L} H inductor and a {R} Ω resistor are connected in series to a {Ev} V battery at $t = 0$. Find the time constant (ms), the final current (A), and the current (A) at $t = {tms:sig3}$ ms, each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\tau = L/R = {L}/{R}$ s $=$ **{taums:sig3} ms**. Final current $\mathcal{E}/R = {Ev}/{R} =$ **{Imax:sig3} A**.

$t/\tau = {tms:sig3}/{taums:sig4} = {ratio:num4}$, so $I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{\,R}(1 - e^{-t/\tau}) = {Imax:sig4}(1 - e^{-{ratio:num4}}) =$ **{I:sig3} A**.

drills.title: LC resonant frequency
drills.prompt: An LC circuit has a {L} mH inductor and a {C:dp0} nF capacitor. Find its resonant frequency in kHz, to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution: $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{({L}\times10^{-3})({C:dp0}\times10^{-9})}} =$ **{fk:sig3} kHz**.

drills.title: RMS values and reactance
drills.prompt: An AC source has peak voltage {V0} V and frequency {f} Hz. Find (a) its rms voltage, (b) the average power it delivers to a {R} Ω resistor, and (c) the reactance of a {C} μF capacitor at this frequency. Give each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
(a) $V_{\text{rms}} = V_0/\sqrt2 =$ **{Vr:sig3} V**.

(b) $P = V_{\text{rms}}^2/R =$ **{P:sig3} W** (not $V_0^2/R$, which is the peak power).

(c) $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi({f:dp0})({C}\times10^{-6})} =$ **{XC:sig3} Ω**.

drills.title: Phase angle and power in a series RLC circuit
drills.prompt: A {Vr:dp0} V (rms), {f:dp0} Hz source drives a series circuit of a {R:dp0} Ω resistor, a {LmH:dp0} mH inductor and a {CuF:dp0} μF capacitor. Find the impedance (Ω, 3 significant figures), the phase angle $\phi$ (degrees to the nearest 0.1°, positive if the current lags), and the average power delivered (W, 3 significant figures).
drills.solution:
$X_L = 2\pi fL = 2\pi({f:dp0})({LmH:dp0}\times10^{-3}) = {XL:sig4}$ Ω and $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi({f:dp0})({CuF:dp0}\times10^{-6})} = {XC:sig4}$ Ω.

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = \sqrt{{R:dp0}^2 + ({XL:sig4} - {XC:sig4})^2} =$ **{Z:sig3} Ω**.

$\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{\,R}$, so $\phi =$ **{phi:num1}°** and the power factor is $\cos\phi = R/Z = {pf:dp3}$.

$I_{\text{rms}} = V_{\text{rms}}/Z = {I:sig4}$ A, and $P = I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi = I_{\text{rms}}^2R =$ **{P:sig3} W**.

drills.title: Wavelength and frequency of EM waves
drills.prompt: An electromagnetic wave in vacuum has frequency ${fm}\times10^{{fe}}$ Hz. What is its wavelength in meters, to 3 significant figures? ($c = 3.00\times10^8$ m/s)
drills.solution: $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{\,f} = \dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{{fm}\times10^{{fe}}} = \mathbf{{lam:texsci}}$ m. (Radio and microwaves have long wavelengths; visible light is a few hundred nanometers; X-rays are far shorter.)

drills.title: Snell's law
drills.prompt: Light in {m1} (n = {m1:num2}) strikes {m2} at {t1}° from the normal. Find the angle of refraction (to the nearest 0.1°) and the speed of light in the second material (m/s, 3 significant figures). ($c = 3.00\times10^8$ m/s)
drills.solution:
$n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$: $\sin\theta_2 = \dfrac{{m1:num2}\sin {t1}^\circ}{{m2:num2}}$, so $\theta_2 =$ **{t2:num1}°** (bent toward the normal).

$v = c/n = \mathbf{{v:texsci}}$ m/s.

drills.title: Critical angle for total internal reflection
drills.prompt: Light travels inside a material with $n = {n1}$ toward a boundary with {out}. What is the critical angle for total internal reflection, to the nearest 0.1°?
drills.solution: $\sin\theta_c = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{{out:num2}}{{n1}}$, so $\theta_c =$ **{tc:num1}°**. Rays hitting the boundary at more than this angle (from the normal) are totally reflected.

drills.title: Light through polarizers
drills.prompt: Unpolarized light of intensity {I0:dp0} W/m² passes through a polarizer, then a second polarizer whose axis is at {th}° to the first. Find the intensity after each polarizer, in W/m² to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
The first polarizer passes half of unpolarized light: $I_1 = {I0:dp0}/2 =$ **{I1:num1} W/m²**.

Malus's law: $I_2 = I_1\cos^2\theta = {I1:num1}\cos^2 {th}^\circ =$ **{I2:sig3} W/m²**.

drills.title: Brewster's angle
drills.prompt: Unpolarized light in {n1} ($n = {n1:num2}$) reflects from a flat surface of {n2}. At what angle of incidence is the reflected light completely polarized, and what is the angle of refraction at that incidence? Give both in degrees to the nearest 0.1°.
drills.solution:
Brewster's angle: $\tan\theta_B = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{{n2:num2}}{{n1:num2}}$, so $\theta_B =$ **{tB:num1}°**.

At Brewster's angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so $\theta_2 = 90^\circ - \theta_B =$ **{t2:num1}°**. (Check with Snell's law: ${n1:num2}\sin {tB:num1}^\circ = {n2:num2}\sin {t2:num1}^\circ$.)

drills.title: Intensity and fields from a point source
drills.prompt: A small source radiates {Pw:dp0} W of electromagnetic power equally in all directions. At {r} m from it, find the intensity (W/m²), the peak electric field (V/m) and the peak magnetic field (T), each to 3 significant figures. ($c = 3.00\times10^8$ m/s, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²))
drills.solution:
The power spreads over a sphere: $I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2} = \dfrac{{Pw:dp0}}{4\pi({r})^2} =$ **{I:sig3} W/m²**.

From $I = \tfrac12c\varepsilon_0E_0^2$: $E_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2I}{c\varepsilon_0}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2({I:sig4})}{(3.00\times10^8)(8.85\times10^{-12})}} =$ **{E0:sig3} V/m**.

$B_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{c} = \dfrac{{E0:sig4}}{3.00\times10^8} = \mathbf{{B0:texsci}}$ T.

drills.title: Radiation pressure and force
drills.prompt: Light of intensity {I:dp0} W/m² falls head-on on a flat surface of area {A} m² that {surf}. Find the radiation pressure (Pa) and the force on the surface (N), each to 3 significant figures. ($c = 3.00\times10^8$ m/s)
drills.solution:
The pressure is $I/c$ on a surface that absorbs and $2I/c$ on one that reflects. This surface {surf}, so $P_{\text{rad}} = \dfrac{{surf:dp0}\times{I:dp0}}{3.00\times10^8} = \mathbf{{Prad:texsci}}$ Pa.

$F = P_{\text{rad}}A = ({Prad:texsci})({A}) = \mathbf{{F:texsci}}$ N.

drills.title: Thin lens image
drills.prompt: A {ho} cm tall object stands {dob} cm from a thin lens of focal length {f} cm (negative = diverging). Find the image distance in cm (negative = virtual, same side as the object) and the magnification, each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f - \dfrac1{d_o} = \dfrac{1}{{f}} - \dfrac{1}{{dob}}$, so $d_i =$ **{di:sig3} cm**.

$m = -\dfrac{d_i}{d_o} =$ **{m:sig3}**, so the image is {hi:num2} cm tall (negative means inverted). A positive $d_i$ is a real image on the far side.

drills.title: Spherical mirror image
drills.prompt: An object is {dob} cm in front of a {kind} mirror with radius of curvature {R} cm. Find the image distance in cm (negative = behind the mirror, virtual) and the magnification, each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$f = \pm R/2$, positive for concave and negative for convex: $f = {f}$ cm.

$\dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f - \dfrac1{d_o}$, so $d_i =$ **{di:sig3} cm**; $m = -d_i/d_o =$ **{m:sig3}**.

drills.title: Two-lens system
drills.prompt: An object is {d1} cm in front of a converging lens ($f_1 = {f1}$ cm). A second converging lens ($f_2 = {f2}$ cm) is {sep} cm beyond the first. Find the final image distance from the second lens (cm) and the overall magnification, each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
Lens 1: $d_{i1} = \left(\dfrac{1}{{f1}} - \dfrac{1}{{d1}}\right)^{-1} = {img1:num2}$ cm, with $m_1 = -d_{i1}/d_{o1} = {mag1:num4}$.

That image is the object for lens 2, at $d_{o2} = {sep} - {img1:num2} = {obj2:num2}$ cm.

Lens 2: $d_{i2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{{f2}} - \dfrac{1}{{obj2:num2}}\right)^{-1} =$ **{img2:sig3} cm**.

Total $m = m_1m_2 = \left(-\dfrac{d_{i1}}{d_{o1}}\right)\left(-\dfrac{d_{i2}}{d_{o2}}\right) =$ **{m:sig3}**.

drills.title: Image formed by one refracting surface
drills.prompt: An object in {n1} ($n_1 = {n1:num2}$) is {dob} cm in front of a spherical surface of {n2}, with $R = {Rc}$ cm (positive means the center of curvature is inside the second material). Find the image distance (cm; negative means a virtual image on the object's side) and the lateral magnification, each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\dfrac{n_1}{d_o} + \dfrac{n_2}{d_i} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$: $\dfrac{{n1:num2}}{{dob}} + \dfrac{{n2:num2}}{d_i} = \dfrac{{n2:num2} - {n1:num2}}{{Rc}}$, so $d_i =$ **{di:sig3} cm**.

$m = -\dfrac{n_1d_i}{n_2d_o} = -\dfrac{({n1:num2})({di:sig4})}{({n2:num2})({dob})} =$ **{m:sig3}** (negative: inverted; positive: upright).

drills.title: Corrective lenses
drills.prompt: (a) A nearsighted person has a far point of {far} cm. (b) A farsighted person has a near point of {near} cm and wants to read at 25 cm. Treating each lens as being at the eye, find the lens power each person needs, in diopters to 3 significant figures (include the sign).
drills.solution:
(a) Distant objects ($d_o = \infty$) must appear at the far point, $d_i = -{far}$ cm: $P = \dfrac{1}{\,f} = \dfrac{1}{-{far}/100\text{ m}} =$ **{P1:sig3} D** (diverging).

(b) An object at $d_o = 0.25$ m must appear at the near point, $d_i = -{near}/100$ m: $P = \dfrac{1}{0.25} + \dfrac{1}{-{near}/100} =$ **{P2:sig3} D** (converging).

drills.title: Compound microscope
drills.prompt: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length {fo:num2} cm and an eyepiece of focal length {fe:num1} cm. A specimen is {dob:num2} cm from the objective, and the final image is at infinity. Find the objective's image distance (cm), the objective's lateral magnification, and the overall magnification (use a 25 cm near point), each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
Objective: $\dfrac{1}{d_i} = \dfrac{1}{{fo:num2}} - \dfrac{1}{{dob:num2}}$, so $d_i =$ **{di:sig3} cm**, and $m_o = -\dfrac{d_i}{d_o} = -\dfrac{{di:sig4}}{{dob:num2}} =$ **{mo:sig3}**.

Eyepiece: $M_e = \dfrac{25\text{ cm}}{f_e} = \dfrac{25}{{fe:num1}} = {Me:sig4}$.

Overall: $M = m_oM_e =$ **{M:sig3}** (the minus sign means the image is inverted).

drills.title: Double-slit fringes
drills.prompt: Light of wavelength {lam:dp0} nm falls on two slits {dmm} mm apart; the screen is {L} m away. Find the fringe spacing in mm and the angle of the order-{mo} bright fringe in degrees, each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\Delta y = \dfrac{\lambda L}{d} = \dfrac{({lam:dp0}\times10^{-9})({L})}{{dmm}\times10^{-3}} =$ **{dy:sig3} mm**.

$\sin\theta = \dfrac{m\lambda}{d} = \dfrac{{mo}({lam:dp0}\times10^{-9})}{{dmm}\times10^{-3}}$, so $\theta =$ **{ang:sig3}°**.

drills.title: Diffraction grating
drills.prompt: A grating has {N:dp0} lines per mm and is lit with {lam:dp0} nm light. Find the angle of the first-order maximum (to the nearest 0.1°) and the highest order that appears on a screen in front of the grating.
drills.solution:
$d = \dfrac{1}{{N:dp0}\text{ mm}^{-1}} = {d:texsci}$ m. $\sin\theta_1 = \lambda/d$, so $\theta_1 =$ **{t1:num1}°**.

A maximum needs $\sin\theta = m\lambda/d < 1$ (an order with $\sin\theta = 1$ would travel along the grating's surface, never reaching the screen), so $m < d/\lambda = {ratio:num4}$. The highest order is **{mmax}**.

drills.title: Thin film color
drills.prompt: A thin film with $n = {n}$ surrounded by air strongly reflects {lam:dp0} nm light. Find the film thickness in nm, to 3 significant figures, for constructive order $m = {mm}$ (where $m = 0$ is the thinnest such film).
drills.solution:
Only the top reflection flips phase, so bright reflection needs $2nt = (m + \tfrac12)\lambda$.

$t = \dfrac{({mm} + 0.5)({lam:dp0})}{2({n})} =$ **{t:sig3} nm**.

drills.title: Time dilation
drills.prompt: A spacecraft moves at ${b:dp3}c$ relative to Earth. A clock on board measures {t0} μs between two ticks. Find the Lorentz factor (4 significant figures) and the time between those ticks measured from Earth (μs, 3 significant figures).
drills.solution:
$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - ({b:dp3})^2}} =$ **{gam:sig4}**.

The ship's clock measures proper time, so $\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0 = {gam:sig4}({t0}) =$ **{t:sig3} μs**.

drills.title: Length contraction
drills.prompt: A spaceship has a proper length of {L0} m. What length do observers measure as it passes at ${b}c$? Give meters to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution: $L = L_0\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = {L0}\sqrt{1 - ({b})^2} =$ **{L:sig3} m** (only the length along the motion contracts).

drills.title: Relativistic energy and momentum
drills.prompt: Consider {part} moving at ${b}c$. Find its total energy (MeV), kinetic energy (MeV) and momentum (in MeV/$c$), each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - ({b})^2} = {gam:sig4}$.

$E = \gamma mc^2 =$ **{E:sig3} MeV**; $K = (\gamma - 1)mc^2 =$ **{K:sig3} MeV**; $pc = \gamma mc^2(v/c) =$ **{pc:sig3} MeV**, so $p$ = {pc:sig3} MeV/$c$.

drills.title: Photon energy and photon rate
drills.prompt: A {PmW} mW light source emits {lam:dp0} nm light. Find the energy of each photon in eV and the number of photons emitted per second, each to 3 significant figures. ($hc = 1240$ eV·nm, $1\text{ eV} = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ J)
drills.solution:
$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1240}{{lam:dp0}} =$ **{EeV:sig3} eV** $= {EJ:texsci}$ J.

Rate $= \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{{PmW}\times10^{-3}}{{EJ:texsci}} = \mathbf{{N:texsci}}$ photons/s.

drills.title: Photoelectric effect
drills.prompt: Light of wavelength {lam:dp0} nm shines on {metal}. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons (eV) and the metal's threshold wavelength (nm), each to 3 significant figures. ($hc = 1240$ eV·nm)
drills.solution:
Photon energy: $1240/{lam:dp0} = {E:num4}$ eV. $K_{\max} = hf - \phi = {E:num4} - {metal:num2} =$ **{K:sig3} eV** (stopping potential {K:sig3} V).

Threshold: $\lambda_0 = hc/\phi = 1240/{metal:num2} =$ **{l0:sig3} nm**.

drills.title: Hydrogen transition (Bohr model)
drills.prompt: A hydrogen atom's electron drops from $n = {ni}$ to $n = {nf}$. Find the energy (eV) and wavelength (nm) of the emitted photon, each to 4 significant figures. ($E_n = -13.6\text{ eV}/n^2$, $hc = 1240$ eV·nm)
drills.solution:
$\Delta E = 13.6\left(\dfrac{1}{{nf}^2} - \dfrac{1}{{ni}^2}\right) =$ **{dE:sig4} eV**.

$\lambda = 1240/\Delta E =$ **{lam:sig4} nm** (visible if between about 400 and 700 nm; transitions to $n = 1$ are ultraviolet).

drills.title: de Broglie wavelength of an accelerated particle
drills.prompt: Starting from rest, {part} is accelerated through {V:dp0} V. Find its de Broglie wavelength in nm, to 3 significant figures (ignore relativistic effects). ($h = 6.63\times10^{-34}$ J·s, $e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, $m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $m_p = 1.673\times10^{-27}$ kg)
drills.solution:
$K = eV$ and $p = \sqrt{2mK} = \sqrt{2({mcoef:sig4}\times10^{{mexp}})(1.602\times10^{-19})({V:dp0})} = {p:texsci}$ kg·m/s.

$\lambda = \dfrac hp = {lam:texsci}$ m $= \mathbf{{lnm:texsci}}$ nm.

drills.title: Wien's law and Stefan–Boltzmann law
drills.prompt: An object's thermal spectrum peaks at {lam:dp0} nm. Its surface has area {A} m² and emissivity {ems:num2}. Find its temperature (K) and the total power it radiates (W), each to 3 significant figures. (Wien's constant $2.898\times10^{-3}$ m·K, $\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/(m²·K⁴))
drills.solution:
Wien's law: $T = \dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}\text{ m·K}}{{lam:dp0}\times10^{-9}\text{ m}} =$ **{T:sig3} K**.

Stefan–Boltzmann: $P = e\sigma AT^4 = ({ems:num2})(5.67\times10^{-8})({A})({T:sig4})^4 = \mathbf{{P:texsci}}$ W.

drills.title: Compton scattering
drills.prompt: X-rays of wavelength {lam:num1} pm scatter from free electrons, and you detect those scattered at {th}°. Find the Compton shift (pm, 3 significant figures), the scattered wavelength (pm, 4 significant figures), and the recoiling electron's kinetic energy (keV, 3 significant figures). ($h/(m_ec) = 2.43$ pm, $hc = 1240$ eV·nm $= 1240$ keV·pm)
drills.solution:
$\Delta\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta) = 2.43(1 - \cos {th}^\circ) =$ **{dl:sig3} pm**, so $\lambda' = {lam:num1} + {dl:sig4} =$ **{lp:sig4} pm**.

The electron gets the energy the photon lost: $K = hc\left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda'}\right) = 1240\left(\dfrac{1}{{lam:num1}} - \dfrac{1}{{lp:sig4}}\right)$ keV $=$ **{K:sig3} keV**.

drills.title: Radioactive decay
drills.prompt: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of {T} days. A sample starts with activity {A0:dp0} MBq. Find the decay constant (per day) and the activity after {t} days (MBq), each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{{T}} =$ **{lam:sig3} per day**.

$A = A_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/T_{1/2}} = {A0:dp0}\left(\tfrac12\right)^{{t}/{T}} =$ **{A:sig3} MBq**.

drills.title: Nuclear binding energy
drills.prompt: Find the mass defect (u), binding energy (MeV) and binding energy per nucleon (MeV) of {nuc}, each to 4 significant figures. Use hydrogen-atom mass 1.007825 u, neutron mass 1.008665 u, and 1 u = 931.5 MeV/$c^2$.
drills.solution:
Separate parts: ${Z}(1.007825) + {N}(1.008665) = {mtot:dp6}$ u.

Mass defect: $\Delta m = {mtot:dp6} - {nuc:dp6} =$ **{dm:sig4} u**.

$E_B = \Delta m\,(931.5\text{ MeV/u}) =$ **{EB:sig4} MeV**, or **{per:sig4} MeV** per nucleon.

drills.title: Carbon dating
drills.prompt: A sample of ancient charcoal has {pct}% of the carbon-14 activity of living wood. Using a half-life of 5730 years, how old is it, in years to 3 significant figures?
drills.solution: $\dfrac{A}{A_0} = \left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/5730}$, so $t = 5730\cdot\dfrac{\ln({pct}/100)}{\ln 0.5} =$ **{t:sig3} years**.

drills.title: Coulomb force between two charges
drills.prompt: Charges of {Q1} μC and {Q2} μC are {rcm} cm apart. Find the magnitude of the electric force between them, in newtons to 3 significant figures ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²). Is it attractive or repulsive?
drills.solution:
$F = k\dfrac{|q_1q_2|}{r^2} = (8.99\times10^9)\dfrac{({q1}\times10^{-6})({q2}\times10^{-6})}{({r})^2} =$ **{F:sig3} N**.

It is repulsive if the signs match and attractive if they differ.

drills.title: Net force from two charges on a line
drills.prompt: A charge of $+{qa}$ μC is at $x = 0$ and a charge of ${qb}$ μC is at $x = {d}$ cm. Find the net force on a $+1.0$ μC charge at $x = {x}$ cm, as a signed $x$ component in newtons to 3 significant figures ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²).
drills.solution:
From the charge at 0 (it repels the test charge toward $+x$): $F_{1x} = +k\dfrac{({qa}\times10^{-6})(1.0\times10^{-6})}{({x}/100)^2} = {FA:sig3}$ N.

From the charge at {d} cm: $F_{2x} = -k\dfrac{({qb}\times10^{-6})(1.0\times10^{-6})}{(({d} - {x})/100)^2} = {FB:sig3}$ N (a positive charge there pushes toward $-x$; a negative one pulls toward $+x$).

Net: $F_x = F_{1x} + F_{2x} =$ **{Fnet:sig3} N**.

drills.title: Field and force from a point charge
drills.prompt: Find the electric field {rcm} cm from a $+{q}$ nC point charge, and the magnitude of the force on a $-{qt}$ μC charge placed there, in N/C and N to 3 significant figures ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²).
drills.solution:
$E = k\dfrac{\,q}{r^2} = (8.99\times10^9)\dfrac{{q}\times10^{-9}}{({r})^2} =$ **{E:sig3} N/C**, pointing away from the positive charge.

$F = |q_t|E = ({qt}\times10^{-6})({E:dp1}) =$ **{F:sig3} N**, toward the source charge (a negative charge is pushed against $\vec E$).

drills.title: Charged particle in a uniform field
drills.prompt: Starting from rest, {part} is in a uniform electric field of {E:dp0} N/C. Find its acceleration (m/s²) and its speed (m/s) after it travels {dcm} cm, to 3 significant figures. ($e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, $m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $m_p = 1.673\times10^{-27}$ kg)
drills.solution:
$a = \dfrac{eE}{m} = \dfrac{(1.602\times10^{-19})({E:dp0})}{{mcoef:sig4}\times10^{{mexp}}} = \mathbf{{a:texsci}}$ m/s².

$v = \sqrt{2ad} = \mathbf{{v:texsci}}$ m/s.

drills.title: Field between two charges
drills.prompt: A $+{q1}$ nC charge is at $x = 0$ and a ${q2}$ nC charge is at $x = {d}$ cm. Find the $x$ component of the electric field at the midpoint, in kN/C to 3 significant figures (positive = toward the second charge).
drills.solution:
Each charge is ${d}/2$ cm from the midpoint. The first charge's field there points away from it, in $+x$: $E_{1x} = k({q1}\times10^{-9})/r^2 = {E1:dp1}$ N/C.

A positive second charge makes a field pointing away from it ($-x$); a negative one, toward it ($+x$). So $E_{2x} = -k({q2}\times10^{-9})/r^2 = -({E2:dp1})$ N/C.

$E_x = E_{1x} + E_{2x} =$ **{E:sig3} kN/C**.

drills.title: Field inside and outside a charged sphere
drills.prompt: A solid insulating sphere of radius {Rcm} cm carries $+{Q}$ nC spread uniformly through its volume. Find the field at {rincm:num1} cm and at {routcm:num1} cm from its center, in N/C to 3 significant figures ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²).
drills.solution:
Inside, a Gaussian sphere of radius $r$ encloses $Q(r/R)^3$, so $E = \dfrac{kQr}{R^3} = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)({Q}\times10^{-9})({rin:num4})}{({R})^3} =$ **{Ein:sig3} N/C**.

Outside it acts like a point charge: $E = \dfrac{kQ}{r^2} = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)({Q}\times10^{-9})}{({rout:num4})^2} =$ **{Eout:sig3} N/C**.

drills.title: Field of a long line charge
drills.prompt: A long straight wire carries a uniform charge of {lam} nC per meter. Using Gauss's law, find the electric field {rcm} cm from the wire, in N/C to 3 significant figures ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²).
drills.solution:
A coaxial Gaussian cylinder gives $E(2\pi rL) = \lambda L/\varepsilon_0$, so $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r} = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}$.

$E = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^9)({lam}\times10^{-9})}{{rcm}/100} =$ **{E:sig3} N/C**.

drills.title: Potential from two charges and work to bring in a third
drills.prompt: Point P is {a} cm from a {q1} nC charge and {b} cm from a {q2} nC charge. Find the potential at P (zero at infinity) and the work needed to bring a $+{q3}$ nC charge from infinity to P, in μJ. Give both to 3 significant figures ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²).
drills.solution:
Potentials add as signed scalars: $V = k\left(\dfrac{q_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{q_2}{r_2}\right) = (8.99\times10^9)\left(\dfrac{{q1}\times10^{-9}}{{a}/100} + \dfrac{{q2}\times10^{-9}}{{b}/100}\right) =$ **{V:sig3} V**.

Work $= q\Delta V = ({q3}\times10^{-9})({V:dp1}) = {W:texsci}$ J $=$ **{Wu:sig3} μJ**.

drills.title: Speed after acceleration through a potential difference
drills.prompt: Starting from rest, {part} is accelerated through a potential difference of {dV:dp0} V. Find its kinetic energy in joules and its final speed in m/s, to 3 significant figures. ($e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, $m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $m_p = 1.673\times10^{-27}$ kg)
drills.solution:
$K = e\Delta V = {dV:dp0}$ eV $= (1.602\times10^{-19})({dV:dp0}) = \mathbf{{K:texsci}}$ J.

$v = \sqrt{2K/m} = \mathbf{{v:texsci}}$ m/s.

drills.title: Uniform field between plates
drills.prompt: Two parallel plates {dmm} mm apart are held at a potential difference of {V} V. Find the field between them (V/m) and the force on a {qn} nC charge there (N), to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$E = \dfrac{\Delta V}{d} = \dfrac{{V}}{{dmm}\times10^{-3}} =$ **{E:sig3} V/m**.

$F = qE = ({qn}\times10^{-9})({E:dp0}) = \mathbf{{F:texsci}}$ N.

drills.title: Dipole moment and the field on the axis
drills.prompt: Charges of $+{qn}$ nC and $-{qn}$ nC are {dmm} mm apart. Find the dipole moment (in pC·m; 1 pC·m = $10^{-12}$ C·m) and, using the far-field approximation, the electric field on the dipole's axis {xcm} cm from its center (N/C). Give each to 3 significant figures. ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
drills.solution:
$p = qd = ({qn}\times10^{-9})({dmm}\times10^{-3}) = {p:texsci}$ C·m $=$ **{ppc:sig3} pC·m**, pointing from the negative charge to the positive one.

The point is far compared with the spacing, so $E \approx \dfrac{2kp}{x^3} = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^9)({p:texsci})}{({xcm}/100)^3} = \mathbf{{E:texsci}}$ N/C, along $\vec p$. (The exact two-charge formula gives ${Eex:texsci}$ N/C: this far out, the approximation is excellent.)

drills.title: Torque and energy of a dipole in a field
drills.prompt: A dipole of moment ${pm}\times10^{-9}$ C·m makes an angle of {th}° with a uniform electric field of {Ek} kN/C. Find (a) the torque on it (N·m), (b) its potential energy (J, taking $U = 0$ at $90^\circ$; include the sign), and (c) the work the field does on it as it swings into alignment with the field (J). Give each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$pE = ({pm}\times10^{-9})({Ek}\times10^3) = {pE:texsci}$ N·m.

(a) $\tau = pE\sin\theta = ({pE:texsci})\sin {th}^\circ = \mathbf{{tau:texsci}}$ N·m, turning the dipole toward the field.

(b) $U = -pE\cos\theta = -({pE:texsci})\cos {th}^\circ = \mathbf{{U:texsci}}$ J.

(c) Aligned, $U = -pE$. The field's work is the drop in potential energy: $W = U - (-pE) = pE(1 - \cos {th}^\circ) = \mathbf{{W:texsci}}$ J.

drills.title: Parallel-plate capacitor
drills.prompt: A parallel-plate capacitor has square plates {side} cm on a side, {dmm} mm apart, filled with {kap}. Find its capacitance in pF and the charge in nC when it is connected to {V} V, to 3 significant figures. ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m)
drills.solution:
$A = ({side}/100)^2 = {A:num4}$ m². $C = \kappa\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d} = {kap:num2}\cdot\dfrac{(8.85\times10^{-12})({A:num4})}{{dmm}\times10^{-3}} =$ **{C:sig3} pF**.

$Q = CV =$ **{Q:sig3} nC**.

drills.title: Capacitors in series and parallel
drills.prompt: Capacitors $C_2 = {C2}$ μF and $C_3 = {C3}$ μF are in parallel, and that pair is in series with $C_1 = {C1}$ μF. The combination is connected to {V} V. Find the equivalent capacitance (μF), the charge on $C_1$ (μC), and the voltage across $C_1$ (V), to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
Parallel pair: ${C2} + {C3} = {Cp}$ μF. In series with $C_1$: $C_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{({C1})({Cp})}{{C1} + {Cp}} =$ **{Ceq:sig3} μF**.

Series parts share the same charge: $Q = C_{\text{eq}}V =$ **{Q:sig3} μC**.

$V_1 = Q/C_1 =$ **{V1:sig3} V** (the remaining {V} − {V1:sig3} V is across the parallel pair).

drills.title: Energy stored in a capacitor
drills.prompt: A {C} μF capacitor is charged to {V:dp0} V and then discharged in {tms} ms. Find the stored energy (J) and the average power during discharge (W), to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$U = \tfrac12CV^2 = \tfrac12({C}\times10^{-6})({V:dp0})^2 =$ **{U:sig3} J**.

$\bar P = U/t =$ **{P:sig3} W**.

drills.title: Ohm's law and power
drills.prompt: A {V} V source is connected across a {R:dp0} Ω resistor. Find the current (A) and the power dissipated (W), to 3 significant figures.

drills.title: Resistance of a wire
drills.prompt: A wire made of {mat} is {L} m long with a diameter of {dmm} mm. Find its resistance (Ω) and the voltage drop across it (V) when it carries {I} A, to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$A = \pi r^2 = \pi\left(\dfrac{{dmm}\times10^{-3}}{2}\right)^2 = {A:texsci}$ m².

$R = \rho\dfrac{\,L}{\,A} = ({mat:num2}\times10^{-8})\dfrac{{L}}{{A:texsci}} =$ **{R:sig3} Ω**.

$V = IR =$ **{V:sig3} V**.

drills.title: Cost of running an appliance
drills.prompt: An appliance rated {P:dp0} W runs {h} hours a day for {days} days. Electricity costs {rate:money} per kWh. How many kWh does it use (3 significant figures), and what does it cost (to the nearest cent)?
drills.solution:
Energy $= P\times t = ({P:dp0}/1000\text{ kW})({h}\text{ h/day})({days}\text{ days}) =$ **{E:sig3} kWh**.

Cost $= {E:num4} \times {rate} =$ **{cost:money}**.

drills.title: Series–parallel resistor network
drills.prompt: A {R1} Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of {R2} Ω and {R3} Ω, all connected to an ideal {V} V battery. Find the equivalent resistance (Ω), the battery current (A), and the current through the {R2} Ω resistor (A), to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
Parallel pair: $\dfrac{({R2})({R3})}{{R2} + {R3}} = {Rp:num2}$ Ω; total $R_{\text{eq}} = {R1} + {Rp:num2} =$ **{Req:sig3} Ω**.

$I = V/R_{\text{eq}} =$ **{I:sig3} A**. Voltage across the pair: $IR_p = {Vp:num2}$ V.

Current in the {R2} Ω resistor: ${Vp:num2}/{R2} =$ **{I2:sig3} A**.

drills.title: EMF and internal resistance
drills.prompt: A battery with emf {Ev} V and internal resistance {r} Ω is connected to a {R} Ω load. Find the current (A), the terminal voltage (V) and the power delivered to the load (W), to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R + r} = \dfrac{{Ev}}{{R} + {r}} =$ **{I:sig3} A**.

$V = \mathcal{E} - Ir =$ **{Vt:sig3} V**; $P = I^2R =$ **{P:sig3} W**.

drills.title: Two-battery circuit (Kirchhoff's rules)
drills.prompt: Three branches connect junctions A (top) and B (bottom). Branch 1: a {E1} V battery and a {R1} Ω resistor. Branch 2: a {E2} V battery and a {R2} Ω resistor. Branch 3: a {R3} Ω resistor alone. Both batteries have their $+$ terminal toward A. Taking $I_1$, $I_2$ as upward currents in branches 1 and 2 and $I_3$ as the downward current in branch 3, find all three in amperes to 3 significant figures (a negative value means the opposite direction).
drills.solution:
Junction A: $I_3 = I_1 + I_2$. Loop 1–3: ${E1} - {R1}I_1 - {R3}I_3 = 0$. Loop 2–3: ${E2} - {R2}I_2 - {R3}I_3 = 0$.

Substituting: $({R1} + {R3})I_1 + {R3}I_2 = {E1}$ and ${R3}I_1 + ({R2} + {R3})I_2 = {E2}$. Solve these two equations simultaneously, for example by multiplying the first by ${R3}$ and the second by $({R1} + {R3})$ and subtracting to eliminate $I_1$.

$I_1 =$ **{I1:sig3} A**, $I_2 =$ **{I2:sig3} A**, $I_3 = I_1 + I_2 =$ **{I3:sig3} A**.

drills.title: Charging a capacitor
drills.prompt: A {C} μF capacitor, initially uncharged, charges through a {R} kΩ resistor from a {Ev} V battery. Find the time constant (s), and the capacitor's voltage (V) and the current (mA) at $t = {t:num4}$ s. Give 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\tau = RC = ({R}\times10^3)({C}\times10^{-6}) = {tau:num4}$ s (**{tau:sig3} s** to 3 significant figures), so $t/\tau = {t:num4}/{tau:num4} = {n}$.

$V_C = \mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/\tau}) = {Ev}(1 - e^{-{n}}) =$ **{V:sig3} V**.

$I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{\,R}e^{-t/\tau} =$ **{I:sig3} mA**.

drills.title: Discharge time of a capacitor
drills.prompt: A {C:dp0} μF capacitor charged to {V0} V discharges through a {R} kΩ resistor. How long until its voltage falls to {Vf:num1} V ({pct}% of the start)? Give seconds to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution: $\tau = RC = {tau:sig3}$ s. From $V = V_0e^{-t/\tau}$: $t = \tau\ln\dfrac{V_0}{V} = {tau:sig3}\ln\dfrac{100}{{pct}} =$ **{t:sig3} s**.
